title: How Night Terrors Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain night terrors (sleep terrors, pavor nocturnus): episodes of terror during deep non-REM sleep (stages three and four) in which a sleeper screams, thrashes, or walks while unable to be consoled and usually remembers nothing. They cover prevalence in children (about 6 percent, ages roughly 2.5 to 12), gender and age patterns, how they differ from nightmares (REM sleep), the sleep stages and delta waves, possible triggers (stress, abuse, sleep apnea, sleep deprivation, migraines, thyroid, full bladder, family history), links to later psychosis, anxiety, bipolar disorder and depression, treatment such as scheduled awakenings and vibrating awakening devices, the dangers of injury including a Phoenix murder case, and a sleep-related augmented reality app. The episode also includes off-topic banter, a sponsor read for Squarespace, and listener mail about memorizing the Gettysburg Address.

segments.title: Opening banter and Squarespace sponsor read
segments.summary: Hosts open with cold-studio banter and a Squarespace sponsor read, then joke about twinkies, fried chicken, and Mary Mac's Tea Room before introducing night terrors.

segments.title: Night terror basics and prevalence
segments.summary: Night terrors are distinguished from nightmares and described as episodes of terror with fight-or-flight response during sleep, with the sleeper unable to be consoled and usually amnesic. Prevalence is about 6 percent of children aged roughly 2.5 to 12, with no gender difference, tapering off by adolescence and rare after age 65.

segments.title: Central nervous system development and sleep stages
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the central nervous system maturing late, then explain the sleep cycle: stages one through four of non-REM sleep, delta waves discovered by W. Grey Walter, and REM sleep with paralysis and dreaming, with cycles of about ninety minutes.

segments.title: Dream recall and nightmares versus night terrors
segments.summary: Hosts discuss why dreams are remembered when waking from REM, and how night terrors differ from nightmares because they occur in deep non-REM sleep and aren't remembered. Brief tangent about Law & Order.

segments.title: Triggers and links to later psychiatric conditions
segments.summary: Possible triggers include stress, sleep apnea, sleep deprivation, migraines, thyroid hormone overproduction, excessive alcohol, unfamiliar sleeping locations, abuse, and family history. A small study linked night terrors to later psychosis, and they can co-occur with anxiety, bipolar disorder, and depression.

segments.title: Treatment: medication, full bladder, and scheduled awakenings
segments.summary: Medication such as benzodiazepines like valium may be prescribed for severe cases; a full bladder can trigger episodes. Scheduled awakenings, waking the child shortly before the usual episode time, are the go-to treatment, and a vibrating mattress device is discussed with mixed reviews.

segments.title: Dangers of night terrors and the Phoenix case
segments.summary: Night terrors can cause injury, including falls and harm to others, and can be fatal in some cases. The hosts discuss the Phoenix case in which a man stabbed his wife forty-four times and tried to drown her, claiming a sleep terror defense that failed, and the death of artist Tobias Long, suspected of occurring during a night terror. Brain activity during episodes is compared to waking violence without inhibition.

segments.title: Cooling sheets, restless legs, and augmented reality app
segments.summary: Hosts mention cooling sheets, a possible link to restless legs syndrome, and an Indiegogo augmented reality horror app called Night Terrors that uses a phone flashlight to scare users in their own homes.

segments.title: Listener mail on memorizing the Gettysburg Address
segments.summary: Listener Matt from Richmond, Virginia writes that memorizing speeches and poems in school is pointless, recalling the Gettysburg Address, Mark Antony's speech, and a poem. Hosts riff on chicken tonight sauce ads.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and email contact information and the website reference.
